title: 10 Types of Cryptocurrency Explained
description:
10 types of cryptocurrency explained in 7 minute.
0:00 - Bitcoin
0:42 - Ethereum
1:26 - Stablecoins
2:07 - Altcoins
2:45 - Memecoins
3:26 - Privacy Coins
4:12 - CBDC
4:56 - NFT
5:39 - Layer-1 Coins
6:15 - Layer-2 Coins

asr.full_text: Bitcoin is the first cryptocurrency ever created, launched in 2009 by an anonymous figure known as Satoshi Nakamoto . It was designed as a digital form of money that could be sent directly between people without needing a bank or government in the middle. Every transaction is recorded on a public ledger called the blockchain, which is maintained by a global network of computers rather than any single authority. The total total of 29 billion coins. This is the minimum value that Bitcoin is contained by a global network of computers rather than any single authority. The total supply of Bitcoin is permanently capped at 21 million coins, a rule written into its code that cannot be changed. Because of this scarcity and its long track record, many people now see Bitcoin as a kind of digital gold, something to hold as a store of value rather than spend on everyday purchases. Ethereum Ethereum launched in 2015, created by a young programmer named Vitalik Buterin along with a small group of co-founders. While Bitcoin was built mainly to move money, Ethereum was built to run programs. Its network allows developers to create what are called Smart contracts, which are pieces of code that automatically execute when certain conditions are met. This opened the door to an entire world of applications, from lending platforms to digital collectibles, to online games. The native coin of the network is called Ether, and it is used to pay for the computing power needed to run these programs. Today, ETH sits at the center of most of the activity happening in the wider crypto space. stablecoins Stablecoins are a category of cryptocurrency designed to hold a steady value, usually pegged to a traditional currency like the US dollar. The idea behind them is simple — regular cryptocurrencies can swing wildly in price, which makes them hard to use for everyday payments or savings. A stablecoin solves this by being backed by reserves, such as actual dollars held in a bank, or by other assets of equivalent value. Popular examples include Tether and USDCoin. People often use stablecoins to move money quickly across borders, to trade in and out of other cryptocurrencies, or to park their funds during periods of market turbulence without leaving the crypto ecosystem. • Altcoins Altcoin is a broad-term term used to describe any cryptocurrency other than Bitcoin. The name is short for an alternative coin, and it covers thousands of different projects with very different goals. Some altcoins focus on faster transactions, some on privacy, and others on powering specific industries, like gaming or finance. Examples include Litecoin, which was created as a lighter and quicker version of Bitcoin, and Cardano, which takes a research-driven approach to building its network. Altcoins tend to be smaller and more volatile than Bitcoin, which means they can offer larger gains but also carry greater risk. Meme Coins bitcoin which means they can offer larger gains but also carry greater risk meme coins meme coins are a type of cryptocurrency that began as jokes or internet culture references rather than serious technology projects the most famous example is dogecoin which started in 2013 based on a popular dog meme and was never meant to be taken seriously over Over time, meme-coins have grown into a real part of the market, driven almost entirely by online communities, social media hype, and the personalities of the people who promote them. Their prices can rise and fall dramatically in short periods, often without any connection to real-world use or development. While a few meme coins have built lasting followings, most fade away once the attention moves on. Privacy Coins Privacy coins are cryptocurrencies built to keep transactions hidden from public view. On most blockchains, anyone can look up a transaction and see the addresses involved, which means activity is more traceable than many people realize. Privacy coins use advanced cryptography to mask the sender, the receiver, and sometimes the amount being sent. Monero is the best-known example, followed by Zcash, which lets users choose between public and private transactions. Supporters argue that financial privacy is a basic right, similar to using cash. Critics, including many regulators, worry these coins can make illegal activity harder to track which has led to them being removed from several major exchanges. Central Bank Digital Currencies Central Bank Digital currencies, often shortened to CBDCs, are digital versions of a country's official money, issued directly by its central bank. Unlike Bitcoin or other cryptocurrencies, they are not decentralized. They are fully controlled by the government that creates them, and their value matches the national currency exactly." Countries around the world have been exploring, or testing, CBDCs as a way to modernize payments, reduce the cost of printing cash, and reach people who do not have bank accounts. China has been one of the most active, running, large-scale trials of its digital yuan while many other nations, including those in Europe, continue to study whether and how to launch their own. Non-fungible tokens Nonfungible tokens, commonly called NFTs, are a special kind of crypto asset that represents ownership of a unique item, rather than a unit of currency. The word fungible means interchangeable. One bitcoin is the same as any other bitcoin but an NFT is one of a kind. NFTs are often used for digital art, music, collectibles, and in game items with each token carrying a certificate of authenticity recorded on a blockchain. They became widely known around 2021, when some digital artworks sold for millions of dollars. Beyond art, the technology is now being explored for things like event tickets, real estate records, and proof of identity. Layer 1 Coins Layer 1 coins are the native cryptocurrencies of their own independent blockchains. Bitcoin and Ethereum both fall into this category, along with networks like Solana, Avalanche, and Cardano. These coins are used to pay transaction fees, secure the network, and reward the participants who keep it running. Each Layer One blockchain has its own rules, speed, and design choices, and are often competing with one another to attract developers and users. Because these networks form the foundation of the wider crypto world, the value of their coins is closely tied to how much activity happens on top of them. Layer 2 Tokens Layer 2 tokens belong to networks built on top of existing blockchains to make them faster and cheaper. As networks like Ethereum grew more popular, transactions became slow and expensive during busy periods. Layer 2 solutions handle many transactions off the main chain and then, settle the results back on it, reducing the load. Projects such as Polygon, Arbitrum, and Optimism fall into this group, each with its own token used for fees, rewards, or governance. They have become an important part of how crypto scales to serve millions of users without breaking the networks underneath them. We covered 10 types of crypto-coins and if you liked it or want to learn on a different topic, please like and subscribe.
